e.t: The word means “pure.” It functions as a describing word, identifying a person, thing, thought, or quality as pure rather than defiled or corrupted. Its central idea is cleanness and freedom from impurity. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times in eight verses, so it is used repeatedly across different passages. The surrounding verse determines the particular aspect of purity being emphasized, but the basic meaning remains “pure.”

e.t: This word means “to choose”—to select one option rather than another. It expresses a deliberate decision or preference, whether the choice concerns a course of action, a way of life, or something considered desirable. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, appearing in Philippians, 2 Thessalonians, and Hebrews. Its precise force in any one sentence depends on what is being chosen and the surrounding words, but its central idea remains the act of making a choice.

Ampliatus is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek New Testament, this name appears one time, in Romans 16:8. The name itself does not provide a further meaning or description of the person; understanding his identity and significance requires the surrounding biblical context, which is not included here. Its use is therefore best understood simply as the proper name Ampliatus.

e.t: This word means “to cause to lie down” or “to recline.” It describes placing someone in a lying or resting position, or settling down for a meal or rest. In the New Testament, it appears six times, each in a separate verse, with occurrences in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. The word can therefore describe either an action done to someone—making that person lie down—or the resulting posture of reclining. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word describes what is genuine and sincere—without pretense, falseness, or a hidden performance. It can describe a person’s character, love, faith, or conduct when these are real rather than merely outward. In the Greek New Testament, it appears six times across six verses, showing a consistent emphasis on wholehearted integrity in Christian life and relationships. Its uses range from sincere love and faith to sincere motives and wisdom. The precise force in any verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but the central idea remains authenticity before God and others.

This word means “to escape”: it describes getting away from something or someone rather than remaining under its power or reach. It is a verb, so it expresses an action rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times, all in 2 Peter. The precise force in each verse comes from its surrounding wording, but the central idea remains escape.

This word means “then” or “therefore.” It connects one statement with what follows, often marking a result, conclusion, or logical next step. In ordinary reading, it signals that the next thought arises from what has just been said, though the exact force depends on the surrounding sentence. It appears 49 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that this linking word serves a regular role in presenting connected reasoning or consequences.

This word describes someone who is ill or sick. It refers to a condition of physical weakness or disease rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs five times, consistently describing people who are unwell. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is straightforward: being sick or physically ill.

This word describes a person who is not greedy and is not loving money. It expresses freedom from a grasping desire for wealth, especially when describing the character expected of a Christian leader or the attitude believers should have toward possessions. The word occurs twice in the Greek New Testament, in 1 Timothy 3:3 and Hebrews 13:5. Its central meaning is a refusal to be controlled by the pursuit of money.

This word means “worthless,” describing something regarded as having no useful value or benefit. It appears twice in the Greek New Testament, so its basic meaning is clear but its precise force in each passage depends on the surrounding sentence. The word occurs in Matthew 25:30 and Luke 17:10, but the reference alone does not establish the full contextual point. Its central idea remains the description of something considered useless or without value.

The word means “must be put,” expressing necessity: something is required to be placed or put in a particular way. It functions as a concise statement of obligation rather than merely describing an action that may happen. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Luke 5:38. The exact force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its lexical sense centers on what must be done. This makes it a word of requirement, marking an action as necessary.

This word means a restraint or restriction—something that holds a person back or limits what can be done. It describes a limiting condition rather than an action or person. In the Greek New Testament, it appears once, in 1 Corinthians 7:35. The surrounding verse is needed to determine precisely how this restraint or restriction functions there, but the central idea remains a hindrance or limit placed on freedom or activity.

This Greek New Testament word means “cost”—the amount that must be paid for something. It names the required expense or price rather than describing the act of paying itself. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 14:28. Its basic sense draws attention to what something will require before a person undertakes it; the specific force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its actual wording.

This Greek New Testament word means “double,” describing something increased to twice its amount or considered in a twofold way. Its basic sense is quantitative: it marks a distinction between one portion and two such portions, or between an ordinary measure and one that has been doubled. The word occurs four times in three New Testament verses, including Matthew 23:15, 1 Timothy 5:17, and Revelation 18:6. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is doubled in each use.

This word refers to something "sacrificed to idols" or "sacrificed to pagan gods." It describes food or another offering connected with worship directed toward an idol rather than toward the true God. As a word used in the Greek New Testament, it appears ten times in ten verses, especially in Acts and 1 Corinthians, where the subject concerns how believers should regard things associated with idol worship. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This word describes people who are frightened or terrified—overcome by strong fear. It presents fear as an intense emotional reaction rather than a mild concern. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, so its meaning is focused and consistent: those described by it are deeply afraid. It appears once in Mark and once in Hebrews, but the precise force in either verse depends on the surrounding passage and verse text.

Because the available lexical information gives only this brief gloss and no verse text, its specific reference in that passage cannot be described more precisely here. Its basic function is a concise ethnic or cultural designation, depending on how the surrounding sentence uses it.

e.t: This word expresses the action of bringing something or someone out, with meanings such as “to deliver,” “to gouge,” “to take out,” and “to take out/select.” Its central idea is removal or release from one place or condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs eight times, including uses rendered as deliverance and as taking something out. The surrounding verse determines whether the emphasis is rescue, physical removal, or selection.

This word means “to foam up,” describing something that rises and froths like bubbling foam. It is a vivid verb for turbulent, agitated movement rather than a quiet or settled condition. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Jude 1:13. Its ordinary sense centers on foaming or frothing outward, and the surrounding verse supplies the specific comparison or force intended there.

e.t: This word means “to name,” “to be called,” or “to call” someone by a name. It describes the act of giving a name or identifying a person through what he or she is called. In ordinary Bible language, it functions as a verb rather than as the name itself. This Greek New Testament word occurs once, in Romans 2:17, so its precise force there depends on the surrounding verse and passage. Its central idea remains the act of naming or being called.

e.t: This word means to touch—making contact with someone or something. It describes physical contact and can refer to an action a person is warned, commanded, or required to perform, depending on the sentence. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs three times: once in Colossians and twice in Hebrews. The surrounding wording determines whether the touch is prohibited, associated with an act of faith, or connected with approaching something dangerous. Its central idea remains direct contact, rather than merely seeing, thinking about, or speaking of something.

This word means “inhabitant of Jerusalem” or “of Jerusalem.” It identifies a person connected with that city, functioning as a designation for Jerusalem’s residents rather than naming a general spiritual quality or action. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, in Mark 1:5 and John 7:25. Its precise reference in either passage comes from the surrounding verse and context, but its basic meaning remains a person from Jerusalem or associated with the city.

Its central idea is deliberate looking that leads to understanding rather than careless observation.

e.t: This Greek New Testament verb means “to accuse”: to charge someone with wrongdoing or bring an allegation against them. It describes spoken or presented charges, whether directed at an individual or brought before an authority. The word appears 23 times in the Greek New Testament, including passages where people accuse Jesus or others. Its basic sense remains focused on making a charge against someone, while the surrounding passage determines whether the accusation is true, false, formal, or hostile.

e.t: This word expresses the idea of being “to be chosen” or “to obtain.” It points either to receiving something as one’s allotted portion or to being selected. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, at Ephesians 1:11. The word’s precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense concerns receiving an assigned portion or being chosen for one. It is not a broad term with many different uses in the New Testament.

This word is the personal name “Quirinius,” referring to a man rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. It functions as a proper name in the Greek New Testament and occurs once, in Luke 2:2. Because it identifies a person, its meaning is simply the individual’s name; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to explain that person’s role in the event being described.

This Greek New Testament word means “word” or “words.” It identifies an expressed statement or saying, whether the reference is to one word or to words together. It is a very common term, appearing 330 times in the Greek New Testament, so its precise force depends on the sentence and surrounding passage. It occurs throughout the New Testament, from Matthew through Revelation.

This Greek New Testament word means “marble,” referring to the hard, polished stone used as a valuable building or decorative material. It functions as a noun naming a physical substance, not a person, action, or quality. The word occurs once in the Greek New Testament, in Revelation 18:12. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning remains straightforward: marble, a costly stone associated with crafted or luxurious objects.

Molech is a proper name for a specific figure named in the Greek New Testament, rather than a general word describing an action, quality, or object. The name appears once in this corpus, in Acts 7:43. Because the available wording identifies the name but does not include the verse’s surrounding text, its precise significance in that passage must be understood from the broader context of Acts 7 and the Scriptures it recalls.

This Greek New Testament word means “alone” or “only.” It marks someone or something as being by itself, or as the single person or thing in view. Depending on the sentence, it can emphasize separation from others or limitation to one person, thing, or condition. The word occurs 112 times in the Greek New Testament, showing that this is a regularly used way to express exclusiveness or singularity. Its exact emphasis in a particular verse comes from the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains being alone or being the only one.

This word refers to an appearance or vision—something perceived as seen. It can describe what is presented to a person’s sight, whether called an appearance or a vision. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times in three verses, with occurrences in Acts and Revelation. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains a visible appearance or vision rather than an ordinary spoken message.

e.t: This word means “to make envious”: it describes causing another person to feel envy toward someone or something. It functions as an action, focusing on the effect produced in another person rather than merely describing envy itself. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in Romans and 1 Corinthians. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central meaning remains the act of making someone envious.

This word means “comfort”: the giving of relief and encouragement to someone who needs support. It names a benefit offered to another person, rather than describing the person who receives it. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in 1 Corinthians 14:3. Its precise role there belongs to the verse’s surrounding context, while its basic meaning remains comfort given to another.

This word means “leopard,” referring to the swift, spotted wild animal. It is a noun naming an animal rather than describing an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Revelation 13:2. The word’s basic meaning remains the animal itself; the significance of its use in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and its imagery, which are handled separately from the word’s ordinary lexical meaning.

e.t: This word means “to obey,” describing the act of following an instruction, command, or authority. It presents obedience as a response to someone whose direction is being given, rather than merely hearing or considering what was said. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs four times, all in four verses: three in Acts and one in Titus. Its exact emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word describes something as full, complete, or containing all that belongs there. It can refer to a quantity brought to its proper fullness, a person completely affected by a condition, or a life characterized by fullness. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs 16 times, consistently expressing the idea of being filled or complete rather than lacking anything essential. Its exact force depends on the surrounding sentence.

This Greek New Testament verb means “to strike” or “to be struck.” It describes the action of hitting something or the experience of receiving a blow, depending on how it functions in a sentence. The word appears once in the Greek New Testament, in Revelation 8:12. That reference identifies its sole occurrence, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain precisely who or what is struck there. Its central meaning remains the giving or receiving of a blow.

e.t: This Greek New Testament word means “far” or “far (away),” describing something at a distance rather than nearby. It functions as a word of spatial distance and can refer to people or places separated from the speaker or from one another. The word occurs four times in the Greek New Testament, appearing in Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its central idea remains distance: being far off or located away from something else.

This word means "gate": an entrance or controlled opening that allows passage into or out of a place. In the New Testament, it is used for literal gates as well as gates spoken of in broader descriptions, so the surrounding passage determines the specific setting. The word occurs 10 times in 9 New Testament verses, including passages in Matthew, Luke, Acts, and Hebrews. Its central idea remains a gate through which people may enter, leave, or be kept out.

This word refers to carnelian, a precious gem or stone. It names a specific gemstone rather than an action, quality, or person. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Revelation, where it is mentioned in descriptions involving precious stones. The basic meaning is therefore a carnelian gem; the surrounding verse and passage determine its particular symbolic or descriptive role. Its two occurrences are Revelation 4:3 and Revelation 21:20.

This word means “mouth,” the opening used for speaking, eating, drinking, or receiving what enters the body. It can refer to a person’s physical mouth and, in ordinary biblical language, can also identify the source or instrument of spoken words. The word appears 78 times in the Greek New Testament, showing regular use across the biblical narrative rather than a rare or specialized sense. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This word means “forum,” referring to a public place or meeting area. It is a noun naming a recognized location rather than an action or quality. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs once, in Acts 28:15. The word itself identifies the place; the surrounding verse and passage are needed to understand the particular circumstances associated with it. Its meaning remains centered on a public forum or gathering place.

e.t: This word expresses being “favored” or receiving gracious favor. It can describe God’s gracious action toward someone, or the act of favoring and giving graciously. In the Greek New Testament, it occurs only twice, in Luke 1:28 and Ephesians 1:6. Its central idea is gracious acceptance or kindness granted to a person, rather than something presented merely as an earned reward. The surrounding passage determines whether the emphasis falls on the person favored or on the gracious act itself.

“Pyrrhus” is a personal name used to identify one individual in the Greek New Testament. It is not a word describing an action, quality, or object, but a name belonging to a person. The name occurs once in this corpus, in Acts 20:4. Its basic meaning is therefore the person’s name itself; the surrounding verse and passage provide the specific details about that individual’s role in the account.
